paras: The attempted lynching of John Nicoli was an attack by a mob on the lock-up at Rochester, Pennsylvania, on the night of September 15, 1888, aimed at lynching Nicoli, an Italian charged with assaulting two little girls. Officers removed him through a back window to the jail at Beaver, and no one was reported killed. The episode reached readers across the country only as a brief Pittsburg wire dispatch.
Nicoli was held in the Rochester lock-up on a charge of assaulting two little girls; the dispatch gives no details of the alleged assault or of his arrest.

On the night of Saturday, September 15, a mob gathered at the lock-up and tried to break down its doors in order to lynch Nicoli. Most printings of the dispatch put the mob at 300, while the Memphis Appeal's version gave 3,000. According to the fuller version carried by the Memphis Appeal, the mob next threatened to burn the building.

The same version reported that "by a clever strategem" the officers got their prisoner out a back window and took him to the Beaver jail. It closed with the remark that "the feeling against the Italian is intense."
No report of arrests among the mob, of Nicoli's trial, or of the outcome of the charge against him appears in the coverage.

The story circulated as a single Pittsburg dispatch, printed on September 16 in Memphis, Salt Lake City, Los Angeles and Seattle. On September 17 it ran in the Sacramento Record-Union's "Telegraphic Brevities" column and in the Silver State of Unionville, Nevada, whose version carried a September 17 dateline and said "last night." The Delta Independent repeated it in a news-brief column as late as September 25.

Most papers ran the item without comment under headings such as "Attempted Lynching," and the Memphis Appeal titled it "An Infuriated Mob." The Seattle Post-Intelligencer instead headed it "A Lecherous Italian in Danger of Lynchling," presenting the charge as established. Every version identified Nicoli by nationality as "an Italian" and described the girls only as "two little girls." The Sacramento brief garbled the dispatch so that the mob appeared to be "at Pittsburg."
The printings disagree on the mob's size, 300 in most and 3,000 in the Memphis Appeal, and since all derive from one dispatch the difference cannot be resolved from the coverage.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Nicoli
bases: A mob tried to break into the Rochester lock-up to lynch a prisoner charged with assault, and threatened to burn the building (A1, A2, A6).

A mob of 300 or 3,000 acted without lawful authority to lynch a man charged with assaulting two girls, but officers removed him to Beaver jail and no one was killed (A1, A2); it was an attempted lynching.
Every report is a version of one Pittsburg wire dispatch (A1, A2, A6); no local or independent account was found, and the versions differ on the mob's size.

accounts.label: Pittsburg wire report (full version)
accounts.gist: A mob of 3,000 tried to break the lock-up doors, then threatened to burn the building; officers slipped the prisoner out a back window to Beaver jail.

accounts.label: Pittsburg wire report (short version)
accounts.gist: A mob of 300 tried to break down the lock-up doors and lynch Nicoli; no outcome given.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the dispatch as a one-sentence item under 'Attempted Lynching' or in 'Telegraphic Brevities' columns, without comment.
The Seattle Post-Intelligencer headed the item 'A Lecherous Italian in Danger of Lynchling', treating the charge as settled, while the Memphis Appeal called the attackers 'An Infuriated Mob'.

conflicts.note: All versions come from the same dispatch, so one figure is likely a transmission or typesetting error; the 300 figure appears in more printings but the record cannot settle it.
The Sept. 16 papers carry the original Sept. 15 dateline; the Silver State's Sept. 17 dateline appears to be a re-dating of the same item, so Sept. 15 is the better-supported date.
